newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel votes 7-1 for for Gingrich reprimand.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel votes 7-1 for for Gingrich reprimand.

text.p: The House of Representatives ethics committee voted 7-1 on Friday night to recommend that Speaker Newt Gingrich be reprimanded and required to pay a $300,000 penalty for his admitted breaches of House ethics rules.
The vote followed release of a scathing report by a subcommittee that conducted a two-year investigation of ethics charges against the speaker. The full House is to vote on the penalty on Tuesday.

Republican Lamar Smith of Texas cast the only "no" vote in the committee, which is equally divided between Republicans and Democrats. Smith said afterward he would have voted for a letter of reproval.

The report said Gingrich agreed that the reprimand and payment to help meet some of the costs of the investigation were appropriate -- one outcome of bargaining between his lawyers and committee counsel on a settlement.
Cole told the committee the sum had to be "high enough to send a message that this was in fact a very serious matter and to get people's attention."
The subcommittee agreed that documents in the case should be made available to the Internal Revenue Service -- an action short of turning them over to the IRS or Justice Department.

If the committee and House approve the penalty, Gingrich would be the first sitting speaker to be formally reprimanded. The speaker is the third-highest elected official of the United States after the president and vice president.

A reprimand, imposed by the House seven times in the past, is exceeded in severity only by expulsion and censure, and the report said the subcommittee felt Gingrich's offences "fell somewhere in between" reprimand and censure.
Reprimand would allow Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, to remain as speaker, but censure could have forced him out.
Gingrich admitted on Dec. 21 that he had provided to ethics investigators "in my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements."
He also acknowledged he had failed to seek legal advice on whether his use of tax-exempt charitable funds for a college course he taught would violate tax laws.
Gingrich said that he had not intended to mislead the committee.

The report said he provided false information in letters that said his motivation for teaching the college course was not political and that his political action committee, known as GOPAC, had no involvement.
"In his testimony Gingrich admitted these statements were not true," the report said. "The goal of the letters was to have the complaints dismissed."

"Only Mr. Gingrich had personal knowledge of the facts ... Either Mr. Gingrich's conduct in regard to the use of (tax-exempt) organisations and the letters submitted to the committee was intentional or it was reckless. Neither of these reflects creditably on the House."
"In addition," the report said, "the violation does not represent only a single instance of reckless conduct.
"Rather, over a number of years and in a number of situations, Mr. Gingrich showed a disregard and lack of respect for the standards of conduct that applied to his activities."
Gingrich has previously received six letters of rebuke from the ethics committee for various infractions.

The report also said Gingrich broke an agreement with the subcommittee not to make statements -- or have surrogates make statements -- about the case following his Dec. 21 admission of ethics violations.
Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner said the punishment showed the speaker was being held to a higher standard than any other member of Congress.
He told a news conference he would vote for the penalty on Tuesday because Gingrich had agreed to it.
House Democratic Whip David Bonior of Michigan, Gingrich's severest critic, told reporters Gingrich should step down but if he did not, Democrats would work with him.
